rivals.statement: Token reach. On hard328 the base's right answers mostly need 4,000-14,000 tokens whatever the prompt or temperature, because the derivations themselves are long. A per-sample cap of 4,096 tokens (and the 7.2 s budget) turns those answers into cap hits, which are abstentions. A vote over 12 capped samples can only choose among problems the base solves within 4,096 tokens, so extra samples cannot reach the long half of the set. Past 16,384 tokens only Think-SFT-like unfinished work still pays.
rivals.readers_wrong: The readers carried over the method's 84/100 dev score and the 'more votes help' rule from MATH-500, where right answers have a median of about 1,400 tokens and the 4,096 cap never binds. On hard328 the cap removes about half of the reachable right answers before any vote happens.

holds_against.why: Doubling the base's cap from 16,384 to 32,768 adds only 4 right answers, which looks as if length does not limit the base. But the claim is about the 4k-16k band: 81 of the base's 164 right answers fit inside 4,000 tokens (result-1b6bf2), so the other half lie between 4,000 and 16,384. Past 16,384 the base's long answers are unproductive, so a larger cap buys little there.

The same 4,096-token capped method reaches 84/100 on MATH-500 dev and ties the cue on the 400 (338 each). On MATH-500 the base's right answers have a median of 1,432 tokens and 263 answers finish within 2,000, so the cap almost never binds there. The mechanism predicts a loss only on long-solution sets.

rivals.statement: Register ceiling. The method's samples come from the plain prompt at T 0.6: a terse, quick-committing register whose hard-problem answers are short, and whose wrong answers on a problem converge on the same problem-specific value. A vote only adds problems where the right value is already the mode. Its ceiling is set by the plain register's per-problem modal answer, about 107 single right at T 0.6, plus a modest vote gain. The 4,096 cap rarely binds on these short answers.
rivals.readers_wrong: The readers anchored on the cue's hard328 single sample (160-164) plus vote gains. But the agent never found the cue: its samples come from the plain T 0.6 register, which scores 107 on one sample, and twelve correlated votes lift that by only about 30.

holds_against.why: Only 43 % of the cued base's vote failures are won by an agreeing wrong group. That is the cue register at T 1.0 on MATH-500. T 0.6 sharpens each sample toward its mode, and wrong values persist when only the sampler changes (fact 27, C - A +0.16), so on hard problems at T 0.6 the plain register's wrong answers agree more.

Only 81 of the cued base's 164 right answers fit inside 4,000 tokens, which suggests a 4,096 cap binds. But those are cue-register answers, long because they deliberate. Plain-register answers are terse (median 609 tokens on MATH-500 at T 0.6), so most of the plain base's right hard328 answers still fit under 4,096.

cell.readout: right answers of 328 under grader v3 (cap hits counted wrong), one sample of the autobench method's own sampling (plain, T 0.6, cap 4,096); compare with the plain T 0.6 single sample at 16,384 (107, result-099916)
cell.why: Mechanism a says the 4,096 cap removes about half of the base's right hard328 answers whatever the register, so the score falls well below 107. Mechanism b says plain-register answers are short and the cap rarely binds, so the score stays near 107. This separates cap against register as the cause of the vote's 139.
